articles.title: Rússia ataca Kiev após Putin prometer retaliação; 6 morrem, há apagões e pontes são atingidas | G1
articles.standfirst: Ataques russos no país deixaram oito pessoas mortas, ao todo, e 28 ficaram feridas, disse o primeiro-ministro Sergii Koretskyi nesta sexta-feira.
articles.summary: Ataques russos no país deixaram oito pessoas mortas, ao todo, e 28 ficaram feridas, disse o primeiro-ministro Sergii Koretskyi nesta sexta-feira.
articles.body:
A Rússia lançou mísseis e drones contra diversas áreas de Kiev durante a madrugada, matando seis pessoas e danificando pontes e infraestrutura de transportes, informaram autoridades locais nesta sexta-feira (20).

Outras regiões do país foram atingidas, deixando 28 feridos, segundo o primeiro-ministro ucraniano Sergii Koretskyi.

Os ataques ocorreram horas depois de o presidente Vladimir Putin prometer retaliar a Ucrânia por três ataques aéreos realizados nesta semana contra a importante Ponte de Kerch, que liga a Crimeia ocupada ao território continental russo.

“Vamos responder a esses ataques, e quero que isso fique claro para todos”, disse Putin a jornalistas na quinta-feira (19), na China, onde participou de uma cúpula com os presidentes chinês e americano. Putin afirmou que a parte rodoviária da ponte havia sido “seriamente danificada” e prometeu reconstruí-la.

A Administração Militar da Cidade de Kiev informou que o ataque atingiu quatro distritos da capital. A ofensiva provocou interrupções generalizadas no fornecimento de energia elétrica. A fornecedora de energia DTEK informou que áreas dos distritos de Pecherskyi, Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi e Darnytskyi ficaram sem energia após os ataques.

Prédios não residenciais foram danificados nos distritos de Obolonskyi e Holosiivskyi, enquanto infraestruturas de transporte e logística foram atingidas nos distritos de Podilskyi e Darnytskyi, informou a administração em comunicado.

O prefeito de Kiev, Vitali Klitschko, afirmou que um ataque com míssil balístico danificou a Ponte Podilskyi, obrigando as autoridades a interromper o tráfego da margem direita para a margem esquerda do rio Dnipro.

Fumaça sobe na cidade durante um ataque de míssil russo, em meio ao ataque da Rússia à Ucrânia , em Kiev, Ucrânia. — Foto: Gleb Garanich/Reuters

A Ponte Darnitskyi também foi danificada, segundo o prefeito.

Outro ataque atingiu a Ponte Sul, onde o tráfego continua restrito. Apenas veículos de até 10 toneladas que seguem da margem esquerda para a direita e transportes públicos de até 18 toneladas estão autorizados a circular, afirmou.

Klitschko pediu aos moradores que evitem se deslocar pela cidade em veículos particulares, a menos que seja absolutamente necessário. Ele também solicitou que empresas e instituições adotem o trabalho remoto sempre que possível.

A Polônia informou nesta sexta-feira que pelo menos um míssil russo atingiu o sudeste do país durante o ataque noturno contra a Ucrânia, e indicou que está investigando outros dois possíveis impactos.

"Há três locais de impacto. Em Nowy Lipowiec, podemos confirmar que se tratou de um míssil Kh-101; no segundo local, também se fala em um míssil; e, no terceiro, o mais provável é que tenha sido um drone a jato", declarou o ministro da Defesa da Polônia, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, segundo a imprensa polonesa.

"Ninguém ficou ferido e não registramos danos a infraestruturas", acrescentou.

articles.title: Conheça o quilombo que preserva  dialeto africano no interior de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Comunidade quilombola surgiu em meados de 1840 em Salto de Pirapora, no interior de São Paulo, e resiste ao tempo com território e dialeto próprio.
articles.summary: Conheça a história do Quilombo Caxambu, de Salto de Pirapora (SP), que preserva sua cultura por meio da Cupópia, dialeto de origem Bantu.
articles.body:
Na zona rural de Salto de Pirapora , no interior de São Paulo, há a preservação de uma cultura quilombola que mantém, até os dias atuais, a memória viva de seus antepassados que construíram o presente. No Caxambu, não há separação entre o ontem e o hoje. Lá, entende-se que o tempo é o guia das tantas realidades que nos rodeiam e coexistem.

O exercício desta visão de mundo não é fácil. Conforme os anos foram passando e a cidade crescendo, as famílias do Caxambu se dissiparam e a manutenção de seus costumes foi ficando mais desafiadora. No entanto, há pelo menos 20 anos, uma nova geração trabalha na reorganização do território e das alianças comunitárias que mantém o quilombo vivo em Salto de Pirapora.

A história do Caxambu é contada por uma geração jovem que aprendeu, desde cedo, a ver e descrever o mundo por meio da Cupópia — dialeto oficial do quilombo. São eles também que, apenas mais tarde, quando deixaram de ser "camanaco", entenderam as responsabilidades de representar o Caxambu e o levou para além do interior de São Paulo.

"'Camanaco' é criança ou inocente, e o vô sempre falava que no 'curima adúfo', nas rodas de batuque, só não podia ser 'camanaco'. Então, aqui tem esse sistema, você passa a aprender as coisas depois que você já entra na fase adulta. É por isso que só quando eu chego nessa fase o vô me chama e começa a falar das coisas mais profundas, que são os nomes dos antepassados, as histórias deles e o significado das cantigas. Isso é muito sagrado dentro da família", conta Antônio Luiz Junior, mestre de Curima Adúfo.

Descendentes do Caxambu mantém viva há mais de 100 anos a história do quilombo em Salto de Pirapora (SP) — Foto: Divulgação

Como uma oportunidade, o g1 teve a chance de conhecer e ouvir, pela primeira vez, algumas dessas histórias da comunidade quilombola que possui mais de 180 anos de existência.

Júnior hoje é um dos porta-vozes da comunidade. Foi ele quem, ao longo da última década, gravou as histórias que Lionel Jacinto da Rosa, o "Vô", contou sobre o Caxambu. É por estes registros que a história da fazenda, dos primeiros ancestrais e da criação do quilombo são preservadas.

Quilombos Caxambu e Cafundó estão localizados no município de Salto de Pirapora (SP) — Foto: Ana Carolina Cirullo/g1

De acordo com os documentos e relatos guardados no Caxambu, os primeiros integrantes do quilombo se uniram em meados de 1840, quando um fazendeiro comprou 12 crianças escravizadas no porto de Santos (SP).

"A gente tem isso em documento e em relatos orais. Mas tudo começou quando o fazendeiro Salvador de Almeida Leite, que não tinha herdeiros, comprou escravizados para trabalhar aqui. Ele compra as crianças e a mais velha, a maiorzinha, foi a nossa primeira ancestral que recebeu o nome de Adelina. E quando ela veio, ela trouxe as memórias da África e ensinou para os mais novos".

Segundo Júnior, o fazendeiro foi orientado pela Igreja Católica a realizar um testamento prometendo a alforria e um pedaço de terra aos escravizados em troca de serviços até o fim de sua vida. Anos depois, com a morte do fazendeiro e a execução do testamento, os libertos tomaram conta das terras e se tornaram quilombolas, estruturando a comunidade na zona rural.

"O Vô Lionel se lembrava de trechos do testamento que foram passados de geração para geração. Ele foi a quarta geração do Caxambu. Hoje, a dona Ana é a quinta geração, a Cíntia, que é a minha esposa, é a sexta geração e as nossas filhas, a sétima. Então essas histórias estão muito vivas".

Lionel junto com os filhos na comemoração de seus 90 anos — Foto: Coçumba Quilombola / Patrick Rosa

A descendência no quilombo se construiu pelas relações que foram se desenvolvendo por todos que dividiram a morada pelas terras da fazenda entre os municípios de Salto de Pirapora e Pilar do Sul (SP). Por décadas, a movimentação econômica da vila se fortaleceu com a passagem de uma rota de muares pela região.

Mais tarde, com a chegada da Estrada de Ferro Sorocabana (EFS), este comércio teve uma queda e algumas famílias quilombolas começaram a se mudar para os centros urbanos que se formavam em Sorocaba (SP) no início do século XX.

"A última família que permanece no quilombo é a família de Vô Lionel e da Vó Susana, uma senhora branca. A família dela chegou ao Caxambu, porque aqui sempre teve a fama de ser muito receptivo. Então, esse fazendeiro, antes dele comprar as crianças, ele já tinha os trabalhadores aqui... Os caipiras, os que os mais velhos chamavam de bugres com miscigenação indígena, né? E a família da avó é um caso desse, que já vivia por ali, muito pobrezinha e eles foram acolhidos pelo quilombo".

Lionel e sobrinhos Jovenil e Marcos durante a gravação do documentário 'Filhos Ocultos do Caxambu' — Foto: Divulgação

Dos costumes preservados pela cultura quilombola, Júnior destaca a valorização de um elemento indispensável para a comunidade: a capela . De acordo com ele, os mais velhos ensinaram a importância deste ambiente com base no que aprenderam com a primeira referência do Caxambu, a menina Adelina.

"O vô conta que Adelina ensinou para os seus mais novos, que durante a vida dentro da fazenda, a capela era onde eles poderiam conversar com os parentes que ficaram do lado de lá do oceano. Então, antes de ser um lugar de religião, é um lugar de sagrado e de ancestralidade".

Nas visitas pedagógicas realizadas no quilombo, o primeiro passo sempre é a apresentação da capela de pau a pique que abriga as fotos dos familiares que já "se encantaram" e as imagens de santos católicos e orixás afro-brasileiros.

Capela reúne imagens de santos, orixás e antepassados do quilombo Caxambu — Foto: Ana Carolina Cirullo / g1 Sorocaba e Jundiaí

Além do respeito ao sagrado ancestral, no Caxambu resiste também o dialeto Cupópia , que já foi interpretada como a "língua secreta dos pretos". Hoje, Júnior explica que, em uma tradução, o termo "cupópia" significa "fala" ou "conversa", e representa uma língua que não possui escrita, pois é transmitida por meio de símbolos e da oralidade.

" O tronco linguístico da Cupópia é o Bantu. E os termos vão se modificando... Por exemplo, sol se diz 'cumbe'. Só que 'cumbe' também pode significar luz, clarão, iluminação. Vai mudando de acordo com com o que você quer dizer".

A Cupópia está gravada também nos tambores, nos artesanatos e nas paredes do quilombo. Esse registro visual é mais uma forma de manutenção do dialeto e seus significados dentro da comunidade. Aprenda mais sobre a Cupópia no vídeo do início da reportagem.

Bancos de tronco de árvore com símbolos de Cupópia — Foto: Ana Carolina Cirullo / g1 Sorocaba e Jundiaí

"Eu acho super interessante que, por exemplo, eles [os mais velhos] trocam essas funções do ensinar. Por exemplo, o pai não vai ensinar cupópia para o filho, o pai vai ensinar cupópia para o sobrinho, para o neto e tal. E aquele outro pai ou aquela outra mãe vem ensinar para outra, para que a as informações circulem. Isso é o que ajuda a manter a história tão rica em detalhes. Porque não parte só de um ponto de vista", revela Júnior.

Em meio a tantos capítulos da história do Caxambu que foram contadas e recontadas ao longo dos anos, um se destaca e ilustra perfeitamente o poder desse fortalecimento do quilombo. Em 2023, mais de 100 anos depois do início do Caxambu, a comunidade recebeu uma visita ilustre de uma realeza.

O Rei Tchongolola Tchongonga-Ekuikui VI, líder do maior grupo étnico de Angola, o reino do Bailundo, veio ao Brasil para uma temporada no país e esteve presente nos quilombos de Salto de Pirapora.

"Eles foram para Bahia conhecer os terreiros da Bahia, eles foram para São Paulo conhecer os quilombos urbanos de São Paulo. Mas no Cafundó e aqui no Caxambu foi diferente por conta da Cupópia. O mais incrível é que o rei conseguiu conversar com os 'griôs' [os mais velhos] por conta da Cupópia ".

Rei do Bailundo visitou quilombos de Salto de Pirapora, no interior de SP — Foto: Coçumba Quilombola / Patrick Rosa

Júnior destaca o dia da visita como um dos mais importantes e emocionantes da história do quilombo.

"Os griôs ficaram muito emocionados por verem africanos, como os tataravós deles, que vieram do mesmo lugar. E a comitiva do rei, eles se emocionam por verem nos griôs a África antiga, que é uma África que não existe mais lá. Então eles chegaram aqui, eles viram a cultura, o jeito de cumprimentar e muita coisa que eles encontraram aqui nos griôs, graças a Adelina que manteve tudo isso. Foi muito bonito".

Lionel Jacinto da Rosa e o Rei Tchongolola Tchongonga-Ekuikui VI, no quilombo do Caxambu — Foto: Coçumba Quilombola / Patrick Rosa

Atualmente, o principal trabalho que mantém a sobrevivência econômica do quilombo é o turismo pedagógico. Além desta abertura para os visitantes, o Caxambu também participa de feiras culturais por todo o estado de São Paulo, vendendo os artesanatos e as cachaças produzidas com uma receita centenária de família.

Os quilombos Cafundó e Caxambu realizam projetos culturais por meio da associação Turi Vimba em Salto de Pirapora — Foto: Coçumba Quilombola / Patrick Rosa

Estas atividades são comandadas pela nova geração do quilombo que une os aprendizados acadêmicos aos saberes cotidianos. Gabriela Delgado é uma destas lideranças jovens que elabora sua história quilombola com sua vivência fora da comunidade.

"Hoje a gente vê que quando uma criança nasce, não dá para você 'encaixotar ela', tipo, 'a criança quilombola tem que ser ativista, tem que...'. É cruel, isso ajuda que a criar a frustração no futuro. E a ideia não é você distanciar, é você perceber que tem como ser as duas coisas. Tem como estar nos dois lugares", pontua.

"Vemos que a cultura quilombola, ela existe em vários âmbitos, ela é muito gigante. Então tudo que você for fazer fora da comunidade, vai ser ancestral também. Esse povo carrega um conhecimento muito amplo, um conhecimento assim, que eu acho que nem se você estudar a vida inteira você vai ter", finaliza.

Lionel junto com os bisnetos na comemoração de seus 90 anos de idade — Foto: Coçumba Quilombola / Patrick Rosa

Neste sábado (21), a Casa Quilomboloa Caxambu irá realizar uma celebração da cultura negra e quilombola, com o tema “Festejar é Resistência”. O evento reúne música, arte, ancestralidade e manifestações da cultura popular, valorizando a identidade e os saberes do povo negro.

A programação conta com apresentações do Grupo Turi Vimba, Bloco Voz do Morro, Samba de Bumbo 13 de Maio, Samba Cláudio Silva, Samba do Laço, Maracatu Terra Rasgada e atividades de capoeira da Casa Quilombola.

O encontro contará ainda com oficinas, artesanato, barracas de comidas, bebidas e gastronomia, fortalecendo o trabalho de artistas, produtores e empreendedores locais.

A festa começa a partir das 14h, na Casa Quilombola Caxambú – Rua Cinco, nº 04 - Boa Vista, Salto de Pirapora.

articles.standfirst: Procissão de 20 anos espera 20 mil pessoas com corda azul, berlinda adaptada e bloqueios no trânsito.
articles.summary: Procissão de 20 anos espera 20 mil pessoas com corda azul, berlinda adaptada e bloqueios no trânsito.
articles.body:
Círio das Crianças 2025 em Santarém — Foto: Arquidiocese de Santarém

O Círio das Crianças 2026 e a transladação movimentam as ruas de Santarém , no oeste do Pará, neste fim de semana. Organizada pela Diretoria da Festa de Nossa Senhora da Conceição, por meio do Setor de Romarias e Procissões, a caminhada religiosa chega à sua 20ª edição e deve reunir cerca de 20 mil fiéis nas homenagens à padroeira.

A programação começa no sábado (21), a partir das 18h, com o translado que sairá da Catedral Metropolitana. O cortejo passará pela Avenida Tapajós, Travessa Professor Carvalho, Avenida Rui Barbosa e Travessa Antônio Justo, antes de acessar a Avenida São Sebastião rumo à Paróquia Nossa Senhora de Fátima, onde haverá celebração de missa na chegada.

No domingo (22), a romaria terá início às 7h, antecedida por uma missa na Paróquia Nossa Senhora de Fátima. A igreja oferecerá um café da manhã aos romeiros a partir das 6h. Como novidade deste ano especial, a procissão contará com uma réplica menor da berlinda com imagem peregrina e uma corda mais fina, confeccionada na cor azul para os pequenos devotos.

O diretor de Comunicação do Círio da Conceição 2026, Luiz Nascimento, ressaltou o papel formativo da celebração para as famílias do município e o propósito de transmitir a devoção entre diferentes gerações:

"Envolver as crianças no Círio é uma forma de cultivar a fé desde cedo e fortalecer a devoção a Nossa Senhora. Queremos que elas se sintam acolhidas e cada vez mais próximas da Igreja, pois são o futuro, mas também o presente da nossa caminhada", destacou Nascimento.

O trajeto seguirá por vias mais amplas para garantir fluidez, passando pela Avenida São Sebastião, Avenida Barão do Rio Branco e Rua Siqueira Campos até a Catedral Metropolitana, onde haverá acolhida e bênçãos. A organização orienta os responsáveis a identificarem as crianças com crachás ou pulseiras, utilizarem chapéus e levarem garrafas com água, apesar de haver pontos de distribuição pelo caminho.

O trânsito ao longo do percurso e nas vias transversais começará a ser fechado a partir das 6h de domingo, de acordo com o plano traçado com órgãos municipais e estaduais de segurança. O cortejo terá suporte médico e de emergência garantido pelo Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu), Cruz Vermelha e Corpo de Bombeiros Militar.

As homenagens infantis preparam os fiéis para a 108ª edição do Círio de Nossa Senhora da Conceição, marcado para 29 de novembro. Na ocasião, a principal manifestação religiosa do município sairá da Igreja de São Sebastião com o tema "Maria Imaculada, Mãe do povo fiel".

articles.title: Saída para o feriadão provoca congestionamento na Ponte Rio-Niterói | G1
articles.standfirst: Travessia chegou a 51 minutos na manhã desta sexta-feira (20). Grande fluxo de veículos também provoca retenções na Avenida Brasil e na Linha Vermelha. Movimentação é intensa na Rodoviária Novo Rio.
articles.summary: Travessia chegou a 51 minutos por volta das 7h30. Grande fluxo de veículos também provoca retenções na Avenida Brasil e na Linha Vermelha. Movimentação é intensa na Rodoviária Novo
articles.body:
A saída do Rio de Janeiro para o feriadão do Dia da Consciência Negra provocava um intenso congestionamento na Ponte Rio-Niterói, no sentido Niterói, nesta sexta-feira (20). Por volta das 9h40, o tempo de travessia era de 39 minutos. O aumento do fluxo de veículos também causava reflexos nas principais vias de acesso à ponte.

Segundo a concessionária Ecovias Ponte, o tempo de travessia no sentido Niterói chegou a 51 minutos às 8h, bem acima dos cerca de 13 minutos registrados em condições normais. Já no sentido Rio, os motoristas levam aproximadamente 13 minutos para atravessar a ponte.

O trânsito também apresenta retenções na Avenida Brasil e na Linha Vermelha, duas das principais vias utilizadas pelos motoristas que deixam a capital fluminense.

Na Rodoviária Novo Rio, a movimentação também era intensa no início da manhã, com passageiros embarcando para aproveitar o feriado prolongado.

articles.title: HC denies relief to IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal; probe reveals family bought 64 villas in Jaipur, 24 of them at Rs 11 lakh each
articles.summary: JAIPUR: Rajasthan high court Thursday declined senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal’s request for interim protection against the Anti-Corruption Bureau
articles.body: JAIPUR: Rajasthan high court Thursday declined senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal’s request for interim protection against the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) investigation concerning the alleged purchase of 64 villas and cottages from a private resort company, Ananta Resorts, owned by Goyal Fashions Pvt Ltd.The villas were allegedly bought in the name of Agrawal, his IPS officer wife Prashakha Mathur, the couple’s two sons and other family members.During the hearing, a single-judge bench of Justice Anil Kumar Upman issued notices to the state govt regarding Agrawal’s petition challenging the ACB inquiry and granted it three weeks to respond. The court scheduled the next hearing for Dec 18.Agrawal’s lawyer claimed that the officer was being wrongfully implicated and sought protection from the preliminary inquiry and any subsequent actions, including the registration of an FIR. The ACB, however, had already registered the FIR against Agrawal, as well as Mukund Saran Goyal and Sanjay Goyal, directors of Goyal Fashions Pvt Ltd, Wednesday.Justice Upman remarked that if Agrawal feared arrest and required protection, he should file an anticipatory bail application. Advocate general Rajendra Prasad, representing the state govt, requested additional time to prepare a reply. The court acknowledged that govt should have the opportunity to respond before considering any interim protective measures, and subsequently declined to halt ACB’s investigation.Agrawal filed the petition on Nov 17, contesting the ACB inquiry. The issue surfaced on Oct 27 after reports said Agrawal, his wife, their two sons and other family members had bought properties from the same company.Probe reveals Agrawal family bought64 Ananta villas, cottages in 2.5 yrsWeeks before Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) registered an FIR against senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal, his sons allegedly bought 24 villas at an Ananta resort in Jaipur for Rs 2.64 crore, at prices far below those listed in the resort’s promotional material, investigators said Thursday.According to the FIR registered Wednesday, the villas were purchased at Rs 11 lakh each at Ananta Resort, Jaipur, compared with a brochure price of Rs 59 lakh for villas of the same size. Investigators say the latest purchase takes the total number of villas and cottages allegedly acquired by Agrawal and his family in Ananta-branded properties to 64 over the past two and a half years. “These things come under the purview of misuse of office and the matter would be investigated before taking any decision,” an ACB officer said, requesting anonymity.The FIR alleges Agrawal misused his official position over nearly two decades to extend undue favours to Goyal Fashions Pvt Ltd, which operates resorts under the Ananta brand, in exchange for financial benefits to himself and his family. The agency said it is examining official decisions from 2006 to 2026, a period during which Agrawal served as Udaipur district collector, chairperson of Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board (RSPCB) and additional chief secretary (industries), among other key govt posts.The FIR outlines three rounds of acquisitions: 20 cottages at the company’s Bujhda resort in Udaipur bought in Oct 2023, in the names of Agrawal and his wife, IPS officer Prashakha Mathur, at Rs 15 lakh each; 20 cottages at Ananta Ajabgarh in Alwar purchased in March 2026 across family members, including 14 villas at Rs 16.5 lakh each, four at Rs 15 lakh and two at Rs 14 lakh; and a further 24 villas in Jaipur purchased last month.A key feature cited by ACB is that the properties were leased back to Goyal Fashions through perpetual lease deeds executed on the same day as the purchases, allowing the company to commercially operate the units while sharing revenue with the owners after deductions.The FIR also alleges that regulatory changes and approvals helped the company overcome hurdles. During Agrawal’s tenure as RSPCB chairperson, the board revised its checklist for Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate on Aug 28, 2023, removing requirements for land conversion documents and forest department no-objection certificates, changes ACB says benefited resorts near forest areas, including properties near Sariska Tiger Reserve. Agrawal later approved consent to establish for the Ajabgarh resort on Dec 12, 2023, and the Damodara resort in Jaisalmer on June 7, 2024, the FIR states.“We are investigating whether these regulatory relaxations, land conversion decisions and investment-related benefits were part of a larger arrangement through which the officer allegedly facilitated the company’s resort projects while his family acquired properties at substantially lower prices,” an ACB ​officer said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Jaipur | Silver Rate in Jaipur | Bank Holidays in Jaipur | Public Holidays in Jaipur | Jaipur AQI | Weather in Jaipur | Petrol Price in Jaipur | Diesel Price in Jaipur | CNG Price in Jaipur | LPG Price in JaipurStay updated with the latest Jaipur news. articles.title: In 2022, Jeff Bezos gave Dolly Parton $100 million to distribute to charities of her choice; the singer had already spent decades building a programme that has gifted hundreds of millions of books to children
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's philanthropic work spans nearly four decades, covering education, childhood literacy and medical research.
articles.body: Dolly Parton's philanthropic work spans nearly four decades, covering education, childhood literacy and medical research. From establishing scholarships for students in Tennessee in 1986 to helping distribute more than 150 million free books through her Imagination Library, the singer has supported initiatives reaching millions of people. In 2020, she also donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for COVID-19 vaccine research, including work linked to Moderna. In November 2022, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos announced on X (Formerly Twitter) that he had selected Parton for a $100 million award, recognising her charitable contributions and leaving her to decide how best to use the money.Jeff Bezos gave Dolly Parton a $100 million award to support causes of her choiceAs reported by Reuters, Parton received the Bezos Award for Courage and Civility in November 2022, shortly after being inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. The award, presented by Bezos, included $100 million intended for philanthropic causes of her choice.During the presentation, Bezos referred to the singer's record of supporting children, education and literacy. He pointed to the range of work she had undertaken through her charitable initiatives, describing her contributions as a reason for selecting her.The award gave Parton considerable freedom over how the money would be used. Rather than directing the funds towards a single organisation or a predetermined programme, the arrangement allowed her to identify causes where the money could make a difference.Accepting the award, Parton said she intended to use it responsibly. She spoke about her long-standing belief that people who have the means to assist others should make an effort to do so, adding that she would try to ensure the money supported worthwhile causes.How Dolly Parton turned a scholarship initiative into a foundationLong before Jeff Bezos recognised her charitable work, Parton had already begun supporting education in Tennessee. She set up the Dollywood Foundation in 1986, with scholarships for students among its first initiatives.The foundation's work eventually grew beyond helping local students. One of its biggest initiatives today is Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, which sends free, age-appropriate books to children from birth until their fifth birthday. What began as a local effort has since reached families well beyond Parton's home state, making children's literacy a major part of her charitable work.Imagination Library crosses the 150 million books milestoneReportedly, the scale of the Imagination Library became clearer in 2020, when the foundation marked the distribution of its 150 millionth book. The milestone reflected years of work involving local partners, families and organisations responsible for delivering books to children.The programme's model centres on making books available without requiring families to purchase them. Children enrolled in participating areas receive age-appropriate titles regularly until their fifth birthday.Literacy has remained a recurring focus of Parton's charitable activities, and the Imagination Library has become one of the most recognisable parts of her work away from the stage. Its international expansion has also given the foundation a reach that extends well beyond Tennessee, where the organisation first began.Dolly Parton's $1 million donation supported Moderna vaccine researchParton's charitable contributions have also extended into medical research. According to her Instagram post in 2020, during the coronavirus pandemic, she donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville to support research into a COVID-19 vaccine.The contribution helped fund teams working on vaccine development, including research connected with Moderna's vaccine. The donation later attracted attention when the role of early research funding in the vaccine's development became a subject of public discussion.Parton had made the contribution at a time when the pandemic was disrupting everyday life and medical researchers were working to develop effective protection against the virus. Her support for Vanderbilt reflected another area in which she had chosen to direct her resources, beyond the education and children's literacy projects associated with her foundation.How Dolly Parton planed to use Jeff Bezos' $100 million awardWhen accepting the $100 million Bezos Award, Parton spoke about the responsibility that comes with having the financial means to help others. She said she had long tried to direct her money towards causes that mattered to her and intended to approach the new award in the same way.The presentation did not announce a detailed spending plan for the funds. Instead, the recognition placed the decision over their eventual distribution in Parton's hands.Her earlier work offered some indication of the areas she had supported, including childhood education, access to books and medical research. However, the $100 million award was not restricted to those existing initiatives, leaving room for her to consider other charitable needs as well.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: BepiColombo spacecraft arriving at Mercury after eight years
articles.summary: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
articles.body:
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.

It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.

Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.

These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."

The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.

With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.

This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.

The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.

If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.

Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.

Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.

But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.

Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.

And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.

The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.

As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.

There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.

Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.

BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.

Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.

"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.

"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."

Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.

Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.

A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.

An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.

A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.

Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.

The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.

"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.

"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."

With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.

Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

articles.title: Bristol Water lifts hosepipe ban, so why are some still in place?
articles.summary: Although the West has had rainfall recently, many supplies remain too low to lift restrictions.
articles.body:
After the summer of record-breaking heat, rivers and reservoir levels have remained low, prompting water suppliers to take action to maintain supply.

Millions of people across the West of England continue to live under hosepipe bans, restricting activities like watering gardens, cleaning cars and filling swimming and paddling pools.

However, recent rainfall meant Bristol Water was able to lift the ban for its customers in Bristol, parts of Somerset and a small area of Gloucestershire.

Wessex Water, South West Water and Thames Water are yet to lift their bans, but have thanked their customers for their continued careful water use.

Although there has been rainfall in the region since the end of summer, many areas are still in severe drought as groundwater and reservoir levels remain low.

A spokesperson for Wessex Water said: "While recent spells of rainfall have been welcome, we need plenty more to make up for the unprecedented dry weather during the summer and at the beginning of autumn.

A spokesperson for Thames Water added that "a sustained period of significant rainfall" was needed before rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels could "recover sufficiently" and restrictions could be lifted.

Meanwhile Richard Stanbrook, South West Water's drought programme director, urged people to "keep using only what you need."

He said: "There's still a long way to go to rebuild our storage heading into next year and the Environment Agency has said England needs at least 120% of its average rainfall over the next six months to be out of drought by spring.

"We're continuing to repair leaks and move water around our network to make the most of the supplies we have while rivers and reservoirs recover."

A spokeswoman for Severn Trent, where there has not been a ban for more than 30 years, said teams carefully "balance the use" of different water sources which "helps make sure water can continue to get to where it's needed."

She added: "We're committed to further improving our network as we look ahead to changes due to climate change and population growth."

"Every reduction in water use helps protect supplies for our customers, communities and the environment," they added.

Severn Trent is the only supplier in the region that did not enforce restrictions on customers.

The company has not had a hosepipe ban since 1995.

Hosepipe bans were introduced across many parts of the country after the UK's hottest summer on record put strain on supplies.

But the Met Office announced that problem began much earlier, as the spring and summer saw five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F), smashing the previous record of 34 days.

The highest temperature of the summer was 38.2C (100.6F), which was recorded at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire on 13 August.

As a result of the prolonged, excessive heat, many reservoir levels reduced significantly and the Environment Agency declared that Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex were all in severe drought.

Bristol Water said it was able to lift restrictions as its reservoirs had reached 43% capacity.

A spokesperson for the supplier thanked its customers for complying with the ban and asked them to "keep up the small habits that make a difference" to help save the "precious resource" all year round.

articles.title: Gurgaon couple buys sandals for Rs 2,429, heel bends on first use, showroom refuses replacement and offers repairs, consumer commission orders full refund with 9% interest and Rs 26,000 compensation and litigation costs
articles.summary: GURGAON: A pair of sandals bought for Rs 2,429 developed a defect on its first use, but when the buyers approached the showroom, they were offered repairs
articles.body: GURGAON: A pair of sandals bought for Rs 2,429 developed a defect on its first use, but when the buyers approached the showroom, they were offered repairs instead of a replacement. Rejecting the footwear company’s repair-only warranty policy, the Gurgaon consumer commission has ordered it to refund the purchase price and pay Rs 26,000 in compensation and litigation costs.Deepak Gupta and his wife Shweta bought the sandals from Stelatoes Shoes & Accessories Pvt Ltd’s Gurudwara Road showroom on Aug 30, 2025. The salesperson allegedly assured them that the footwear was a fresh piece and carried a six-month replacement warranty in case of any defect.However, when Shweta wore the sandals for the first time on Sept 1, the heel bent and the adhesive came loose, the couple alleged. They returned to the showroom on Sept 3, but the manager allegedly blamed the damage on her twisting her foot and refused to replace the footwear, offering only repairs.After their repeated requests for a refund went unanswered, the couple approached the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.Advocate Chandan Yadav, representing the complainants, relied on their affidavit, purchase invoice and photographs of the sandals. The company’s authorised representative, Akshay Sharma, argued that the terms printed on the invoice excluded refunds and allowed only repairs within the 90-day warranty period. He said the company was willing to repair the footwear.The commission, headed by president Sanjeev Jindal with members Jyoti Siwach and Khushwinder Kaur, rejected the defence, observing that a company could not benefit from its own wrongdoing after selling poor-quality goods. It held that unilateral warranty conditions placing consumers at a disadvantage could not override their rights.The panel also noted that the company failed to produce any evidence to rebut the complainants’ allegations. Holding that the company had committed deficiency in service and adopted an unfair trade practice, it allowed the complaint.The opposite parties were directed to refund Rs 2,428.99 with 9% annual interest from Aug 30, 2025, and pay Rs 15,000 for mental harassment and Rs 11,000 towards litigation expenses.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: Apollo 12 was struck by lightning twice after launch; a year-old test helped John Aaron recognise the bad telemetry and tell the crew, “SCE to AUX”
articles.summary: Discover how NASA engineer John Aaron's quick thinking and a year-old test saved the Apollo 12 mission from disaster after it was struck by lightning twice shortly after launch.
articles.body: On the morning of 14 November 1969, Apollo 12 lifted off against a dark, rainy sky. Less than a minute later, lightning struck the rocket. As NASA's history article ‘50 Years Ago: Return to the Moon’ explains, the rocket was struck twice, and a young engineer named John Aaron helped save the day. Apollo 12 carried Pete Conrad, Richard Gordon and Alan Bean on NASA's second moon landing mission. Aaron’s fix was a rarely used switch.A smooth start that turned scaryIt was an ambitious mission. Apollo 12 aimed for a pinpoint landing in the Ocean of Storms near the robotic craft Surveyor 3 that had been sitting there since 1967. Everything was going smoothly for the first 36 seconds after takeoff. Conrad himself described it as a lovely liftoff. Then things went horribly wrong. As the rocket was flying at 6,600 feet and passing through cloud cover, lightning struck. Conrad saw a bright flash, and then most of the spacecraft’s electronics went offline, including three fuel cells powering it. The data on the controllers’ screens in Mission Control turned into gibberish. The second strike, at about 52 seconds into the flight, disabled the spacecraft's guidance system. Fortunately, the Saturn V rocket that was controlling the launch kept working normally.The engineer who remembered Flight director Gerry Griffin turned to John Aaron, a young engineer at the console that monitored the spacecraft's electrical, environmental and communications systems. Aaron’s data had gone from normal to gibberish. But he remembered a test from a year earlier, when he had seen similar signals. He worked out that a unit called the Signal Conditioning Equipment, or SCE, had suffered some sort of upset. A switch, rarely used, had to be moved from its normal position to auxiliary. Aaron told Griffin, who then had astronaut Jerry Carr call it up to the crew. According to Johannes Kemppanen’s Apollo Flight Journal essay, ‘More than SCE to AUX,’ Carr sent the message one minute and 36 seconds into the flight. Conrad was puzzled, but Alan Bean recalled that the switch was on his panel. He flipped it, and within seconds Aaron reported good data.What the switch really did The SCE collects sensor readings and sends them to Mission Control. It has two internal power supplies. The essay explains that the strike probably took out the main power source. The transition to AUX made the device use the backup source, making the figures visible again. Aaron's quick action restored the telemetry. The essay also provides some additional details. The crew could still read key power gauges inside the cabin, and Mission Control could communicate with them via radio. Kemppanen adds that the loss of telemetry itself was not a reason to abort the flight. What the fix gave Mission Control, he notes, was just some extra confidence at a tense moment.Back on track right away Apollo 12 was in a near-circular orbit around the Earth about 11 and a half minutes after launch. For the next two and a half hours, the crew and Mission Control checked every system. Carr then informed the crew they were go for the burn to send them toward the Moon. Conrad joked that NASA needed to do a little more all-weather testing. Apollo 12 touched down on the Moon on 19 November 1969. The Flight Journal essay notes that the launch rules were changed afterwards so that no launch would be attempted in conditions where lightning was a possibility. Apollo 12 remained the only Apollo mission struck by lightning in flight. In the end, a year-old test, recalled under pressure, helped keep the mission on track.You use AI every day. articles.title: Operation Monsoon Thunder:  NCB raids four cities, arrests six in probe into US-bound opioid and psychotropic drug shipments
articles.summary: New Delhi: In a sweeping international crackdown, the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) and the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have dismantled the
articles.body: New Delhi: In a sweeping international crackdown, the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) and the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have dismantled the Indian nerve center of a massive transnational drug syndicate — shutting down an illicit pipeline flooding American streets with deadly opioids and psychotropic substances.​Under an operation code named, Monsoon Thunder, NCB teams carried out raids across multiple Indian cities —including Hyderabad, Delhi, Kolkata, and Lucknow — resulting in the arrest of six individuals linked to the network.The raids were carried on Nov 4 and Nov 13. According to investigative findings, the syndicate operated across borders to supply controlled drugs to buyers throughout the United States.Digital records and examined evidence indicate that the group handled nearly 3,000 parcels containing approximately five lakh tablets between June 2022 and November 2026.During the probe, NCB also flagged several active consignments holding more than 1,500 tablets bound for U.S. destinations and shared actionable intelligence with the DEA, which subsequently seized two shipment consignments.Investigators found that Indian operators took orders via encrypted and messaging platforms such as Telegram, Skype, and WhatsApp, while the U.S.-based arm dispatched shipments through postal and delivery networks, including the United States Postal Service (USPS).Consignment and buyer information was tracked in shared digital records, including Google Sheets. Authorities uncovered a vast customer database covering more than 59,000 subjects—containing transaction histories, past shipment details, delivery addresses, USPS tracking IDs, and drug types—which has been handed over to the DEA to support ongoing intelligence analysis and enforcement against U.S. buyers and drop-shippers.Financial probes show that Indian operators collected payments and commissions through multiple channels, including Venmo, UPI, cryptocurrency, third-party bank accounts, and hawala networks.Investigators are tracing these financial flows to identify ultimate beneficiaries and map illicit proceeds. Additionally, digital files and medicine brand details recovered from an arrested operative point to potential sourcing from several countries, prompting further investigation into procurement channels and international movement.NCB officials said the operation highlights ongoing efforts to counter syndicates abusing digital tools, postal systems, and cross-border supply chains for illicit pharmaceutical trafficking, reaffirming commitment to coordinated international enforcement against narcotic and psychotropic drug networks.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Karthigai Deepam row: SC allows one-time lamp lighting atop Thiruparankundram hill on November 24
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has permitted the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar on Thiruparankundram
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has permitted the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar on Thiruparankundram Hill in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, on November 24, 2026, as an interim arrangement.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi, however, stayed portions of the Madras high court judgment that had upheld the direction to restore the practice of lighting the lamp at the Deepathoon. The interim permission comes amid a dispute between Hindu worshippers and the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah over ownership of the hilltop and the location of the ritual.The development follows arguments by the dargah before the top court on Thursday, when it claimed ownership of the entire hilltop and opposed the demand to light the lamp at the stone pillar. The hearing on the matter had remained inconclusive, with the court scheduled to continue proceedings on Friday.Senior advocate Amit Anand Tiwari, appearing for the dargah, referred to a 1920 judicial order passed in a civil suit and said there were findings establishing that the flight of stairs from Nellithope to the hill belonged to the shrine."The entire top of the hill belongs to the dargah. There is no question of lighting the deepam at the top of the hill, where the stone pillar is situated, irrespective of what the distance between the dargah and the stone pillar is," Tiwari said.He also submitted that the "whole of the top of the hillock on which the mosque and the flagstaff stand" as well as the stone pillar are located is the property of the dargah.What is the Karthigai Deepam disputeThe controversy centres on the location of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lighting ceremony at the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple in Thiruparankundram. For decades, the festival lamp has been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple on the lower slopes of the hill.Hindu groups have sought permission to light the lamp at the Deepathoon, an ancient stone pillar higher up the hill and around 50 metres from the dargah. The dispute has led to legal proceedings over the location of the ritual and ownership of the hill.The Tamil Nadu government had opposed the demand, arguing that permitting the lighting of the lamp near the dargah could create wider legal and administrative complications. On Wednesday, it told the Supreme Court that allowing the practice could lead to thousands of survey pillars across the country acquiring a religious character.The dargah committee had also challenged the procedure followed by the Madras High Court. Senior advocate Huzefa Ahmadi, appearing for the committee, argued that a single-judge bench had passed its order without giving the dargah adequate time to file a reply under the high court rules. He also submitted that the judge had conducted a site visit without notifying the dargah before passing the order.Tamil Nadu government opposes ASI takeoverThe Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) department has opposed a petition seeking to bring the temple and the entire Thiruparankundram hill under the control of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI).In an affidavit before the Supreme Court, HR&CE Commissioner T G Vinay said the temple's ownership and existing religious practices had been settled through decades of judicial proceedings. He maintained that the hill was owned by the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple to the extent recognised by a civil court decree of 1923, which was subsequently restored by the Privy Council in 1931.The affidavit opposed three reliefs sought by petitioner Hindu Dharma Parishad: handing over the entire temple and hill to the ASI, keeping a lamp burning round the clock at the stone pillar described as the Deepathoon, and illuminating the entire hill with lamps during Karthigai Deepam."A title so settled cannot be disturbed and the administration of a religious endowment entrusted by statute to the HR&CE cannot be wrested away and handed over to the ASI upon a petition that pleads no ground in law and seeks the relief in the teeth of a concluded civil adjudication of title," the affidavit had said.On the lighting ceremony, the HR&CE commissioner maintained that the festival lamp had traditionally been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple, and not at the hilltop or the stone pillar.The department also referred to historical records of attempts made in 1862 and 1912 to light lamps near the hill's summit, where the dargah is situated. It argued that archaeological protection at Thiruparankundram covered specified features, including the rock-cut cave and inscriptions, and did not extend to the entire hill or the functioning temple.The department cautioned that allowing lamps to be lit at multiple locations, particularly near the dargah, could disrupt existing arrangements and create law-and-order challenges at a site with a history of communal tension.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Reform selects Robert Jenrick to fight to keep Newark seat
articles.summary: Jenrick won the seat as a Conservative MP in 2014 but joined Reform UK in January this year.
articles.body:
MP Robert Jenrick has been reselected as Reform UK's candidate for the Newark seat in the next general election.

Jenrick had represented the Nottinghamshire constituency as a Conservative MP from 2014, before joining Reform in January this year.

There had been recent speculation that Jenrick would attempt to move to another seat for the next election, although he had previously said he intended to stand again in Newark.

On Friday, Reform's economic spokesman confirmed he had been reselected by his party to fight to keep his seat.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: "Robert is a formidable campaigner and one of the most hardworking MPs in Britain.

"He only got re-elected in 2024, against the odds, because of strength of support he has in the community.

"He has a deep connection with the people he represents, and we know he will continue to be a powerful voice for Newark and one of the most influential politicians in Britain."

Jenrick was sacked by Kemi Badenoch for plotting to defect to Nigel Farage's party hours before the official announcement by Reform in January.

He was first elected in a by-election to the Nottinghamshire seat in in 2014, with a majority of 7,400 votes.

In 2024, Jenrick held the seat as as a Tory, with a majority of just over 3,500 votes.

His defection earlier this year meant it was the first time Nottinghamshire had no Conservative representation in Parliament since 1970.

Last week, the Conservatives selected former Sherwood MP Sir Mark Spencer to contest the Newark seat.

Spender was the MP for Sherwood for 14 years but lost his seat to Labour at the last general election.

articles.title: Palmer Luckey wants Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO: He was on the side of Chinese AI companies, but …
articles.summary: Palmer Luckey wants Jensen Huang back at Nvidia.
articles.body: Palmer Luckey wants Jensen Huang back at Nvidia. Speaking at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, the Anduril co-founder said he disagreed with Huang on whether the US should export chips to China. However, he still called for Huang’s return, arguing that the former Nvidia CEO’s departure served Beijing’s interests.“The bizarre thing that people don’t get is Jensen was basically on the side of Chinese AI companies, but not the Chinese government,” Luckey said. He argued that Chinese AI companies wanted to buy Nvidia’s chips, while Beijing wanted those companies to rely on processors made in China. That distinction was central to Luckey’s case for bringing Huang back, even though he opposed the sales himself.Read what Palmer Luckey said about Nvidia’s Jensen Huang situationAt NYT’s DealBook Summit, Luckey said: “What I said is that China wants Jensen out, so I want him in. And to be clear, I don’t actually agree with Jensen on very material ideas that he has about what the U.S. relationship should be with the Chinese economy. I don’t think that we should be exporting chips to China. He thinks that there’s an argument. I think these are reasonable arguments. There’s other smart people I know, including in the administration, who agree with them. I just happen to not be quite on their side.There’s a lot of people who hear that, and it’s like the midwit take. They say, ‘Palmer, Nvidia is the one that was helping China. So you’re an idiot.’ And what they don’t understand is China doesn’t want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies. There are Chinese companies that want to buy Nvidia GPUs. There’s 600,000 H200 GPUs sitting in a port right now because China will not give them an import permit, because they want to build an internal domestic processor industry, silicon industry, not build one that is dependent on the United States.And so the point that I’ve made is China is thrilled to have Jensen, who is somebody who is pro-selling into—and they’ll say, ‘But Jensen was helping smuggle into China.’ Yes, against the Chinese government’s will. The bizarre thing that people don’t get is Jensen was basically on the side of Chinese AI companies, but not the Chinese government. And so they’re thrilled to have Jensen out. And they know this also: there’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know that it makes America weaker to knock him out.And I’m sure this CFO lady, they put it as interim CEO, is a perfectly wonderful woman, but she is not Jensen, and she is not going to lead them into a period of prosperity that persists for a millennium. It’s just, she’s not quite the right person. Jensen is the guy who built this company from scratch. He deeply understands it. His personal relationships are the reasons that everyone is willing to do business, because paper means nothing. Paper gives you the right to sue somebody after you think they screwed you. That doesn’t actually solve problems. A piece of paper that says I can sue the guy who screwed me, it doesn’t actually solve the issue.Nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture. And so again, China wants him out. Therefore I want him in. But he shouldn’t have slept with whatever she turns out to be.”Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: ‘It just hits me right in the neck’: ‘Evil owl’ terrorises US state, multiple attacks reported
articles.summary: An aggressive owl has been attacking residents in a Massachusetts neighbourhood in the US, leaving at least a dozen people reporting strikes to their
articles.body: An aggressive owl has been attacking residents in a Massachusetts neighbourhood in the US, leaving at least a dozen people reporting strikes to their heads and necks. The attacks have been reported in Brookline, a town south of Boston, prompting local police to alert state wildlife officials and seek guidance on how to deal with the bird.The Brookline Police Department has received three or four calls about the owl swooping down on pedestrians and scratching them, according to a report by CBS Boston. Police have informed wildlife authorities about the incidents and are awaiting further instructions, Boston 25 News reported.Several residents have described being struck without warning while walking or running through the neighbourhood. Brookline News reporter Milena Fernsler, who was among those attacked, told PEOPLE that she was hit twice near her apartment on the Brookline-Brighton border.Residents describe sudden attacks by owlOne of the victims, Taris Besse, told CBS Boston that the bird struck him on the neck while he was outside."Out of nowhere, it just hits me right in the neck. I heard it above me, so it definitely came right from the tree above me," Besse said.He subsequently went to the hospital and received rabies treatment as a precaution. Recalling his visit for a booster dose, Besse said a nurse recognised him as another victim of the owl attacks."For my first booster dose going back to the hospital, the nurse said, 'Oh, are you one of the other ones who got attacked by the owl?' Then I laughed," he told CBS Boston.Juliette Daily, another resident, told Boston 25 News that she was running along Dean Road when she felt something hit the top of her head. Initially believing it was a tree branch, she soon realised that a bird was responsible."It turned around and came back towards me. That time I actually ducked and it missed me, and it tried to go for a third pass," Daily recalled. She eventually ran across the street to escape the bird.Brookline News reporter Fernsler also described being struck twice. Recounting her experience, she said a "forceful whack" caused a sharp pain at the back of her head. She later spotted the owl perched on a telephone pole against the moonlit sky.Fernsler subsequently put up posters across the neighbourhood asking, "Have you been attacked by an owl?" in an effort to find other victims. She received around a dozen reports from people who said they had encountered the bird, according to Brookline News.Why could the owl be attacking people?The earliest reported incidents date back to last fall, with several attacks taking place within a short period around Halloween, Brookline News reported.Massachusetts is home to eight owl species, all of which are protected under state law, according to the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife).Although aggressive behaviour in owls is uncommon, the birds can become defensive when protecting a nearby nest, CBS Boston reported, citing MassWildlife.Police have contacted state wildlife officials for guidance on managing the situation as reports of attacks continue to emerge.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump appears nearly 200 times in Biden’s memoir, book revisits bitter 2024 presidential race
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump may have succeeded Joe Biden in the White House, but he has also loomed large over the former US president’s account of his time
articles.body: US president Donald Trump may have succeeded Joe Biden in the White House, but he has also loomed large over the former US president’s account of his time in office. Biden mentions Trump nearly 200 times in his new memoir, “Promise Me, America”, repeatedly returning to the political rival whose return to power followed Biden’s withdrawal from the 2024 presidential race.The memoir, released on Wednesday, revisits revisits his four years in the White House, his legislative record, the Covid-19 pandemic, the US withdrawal from Afghanistan, the wars in Ukraine and Israel, and his decision to seek re-election in 2024 before withdrawing from the race.The Washington Post noted that Biden had initially sought to avoid drawing attention to Trump when he took office. Five years later, however, the Republican's name appears nearly 200 times in the memoir.The book, released almost two years after Biden left office, also offers him an opportunity to defend his decisions and revisit the pressure from fellow Democrats to abandon his re-election campaign after his debate performance against Trump in June 2024.The frequency of the references comes against the backdrop of Trump’s own repeated focus on his predecessor. Reuters reported in September that Trump had invoked Biden’s name nearly 900 times this year, averaging three mentions a day across speeches, public remarks and Truth Social posts. He blamed the former president for issues ranging from inflation and immigration to munitions shortages, even as Biden had largely withdrawn from public life.Biden stands by 2024 re-election bidBiden makes no apology for seeking a second term, arguing that he believed he was best placed to defeat Trump.“The primaries sent no warning signs that I was in trouble,” he writes. “But that couldn’t derail the narrative setting in on my candidacy. That I was too old. That I was declining mentally.”Recalling the presidential debate in Atlanta, Biden says he had questioned his advisers about whether debating Trump was necessary.“It’s not that I was concerned about my ability to debate Donald Trump,” he writes. “It was that he was so prone to lying with abandon, bullying the moderators, violating the rules, whining about even a hint of fact checking, that I didn’t know whether there would be any value in my giving a public platform to this behavior.”Biden also acknowledges his stumble while discussing the federal deficit, when he said, “We finally beat Medicare,” instead of “We finally beat Big Pharma”, referring to his administration’s efforts to negotiate lower prescription drug prices.“Ironically, this historic achievement wouldn’t lift my candidacy. It would help to sink it,” he writes.He recalls senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer urging him to leave the race, saying it was “personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me”.Trump looms over Biden’s account of presidencyThe Washington Post analysis noted that Trump appears more frequently in the memoir than other prominent figures. Vice president Kamala Harris is mentioned around 50 times, while former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi receives fewer than 30 mentions.Biden praises Harris's 2024 campaign, describing her as “a first-rate candidate” who “performed masterfully in her debate with President Trump”.He also criticises Trump over the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack and his pardons of those involved. Newsweek reported that the memoir also recalls a handwritten letter Trump left for Biden on the Resolute Desk before leaving office in January 2021. Biden describes the note as “beguiling”.The memoir revisits Biden’s defence of the Afghanistan withdrawal and his support for Israel, while acknowledging tensions with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “He and I could be direct with each other, but there wasn’t a ton of trust,” Biden writes, according to news agency AP.The memoir adds to the debate over Biden’s legacy, his decision to seek a second term and the political impact of Trump’s return to the White House.You use AI every day. articles.title: Babydoll singer Jamie Miller covers It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas
articles.summary: It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas for the number one hitmaker from Cardiff.
articles.body:
After spending four weeks at number one in the UK singles charts, Jamie Miller is releasing his take on the festive classic It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas.

In October, Miller became the first artist from Wales to top the UK singles chart since 2011 with his TikTok-viral song Babydoll.

The success transformed Miller's career, but he revealed that his "made it" moment was telling his taxi driver dad and cleaner mum they could retire.

While Babydoll's popularity continues, Miller teased the release of his next track on social media, telling fans: "You guys asked for a Christmas song..."

His cover arrives as artists compete for this year's Christmas number one.

Among those in the running is singer Sam Fender, who covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want in this year's John Lewis Christmas advert.

Other festive releases include Olivia Rodrigo's original Christmas song Take me Home (4 Christmas).

Classic Christmas songs also tend to return to the charts in the lead-up to the holiday, like the 1984 Wham! hit Last Christmas which is currently sitting at number 22.

The song made history in 2023 when, 39 years after release, it reached the Christmas number one spot for the first time, only to do so again the following year.

Regardless of the outcome of the Christmas charts, it is clear the success of Babydoll has had an enormous impact on the singer's life.

He previously shared with the BBC that "nothing feels normal" after the success of the track.

The star said Babydoll came after "a really, really hard few years in my personal life" and with almost 10 years of trying to make it in the industry, he had decided to give it one "last chance".

Miller praised his mum, Anne, when he appeared on the podcast The Person Who Believed in Me for her unwavering support.

He said that, during his childhood, other boys were interested in football and rugby, and there was "bullying" that came with pursuing singing.

But he said his mum would encourage him to "just to ignore people and to keep going".

"She's just the best thing that's ever happened to me," Miller said.

He also credited Anne for helping him get out of the "dark headspace" he was in some years ago: "There was a point where I didn't want to be here anymore. Being in that mind-frame was really scary."

He said she flew to the United States where he was living to spend time with him, and her love for him, expressed in "going on beach walks, going to grab me a coffee, pulling me out of bed", was what "got him out".

Miller also disclosed that money was something he had worried about throughout his life, adding the moment he knew he had "made it" was when he earned enough to help his parents retire.

The singer said his mum had "served everybody else for so long" and talked excitedly about calling her to say: "By the way Mum, you never have to work again."

Miller said his mum was a cleaner who suffered from arthritis, and all he wanted to do was "take those products out of her hands and give her the life she deserves".

The artist, who describes his style as "future-vintage pop", will join a host of singers who have covered It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas, including Bing Crosby and Michael Bublé.

The song, first recorded by Perry Como and The Fontane Sisters, is a festive staple despite never reaching Christmas number one.

It remains to be seen whether Miller could change this, and the announcement of who has topped the Christmas chart will come on BBC Radio 1 Christmas Day.

Miller's cover of It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas is released on Friday. 20 November.

articles.title: 'Compensating with terror': Russia hits Ukraine with 400 drones, 110 missiles in one of war's largest attacks
articles.summary: Ukraine said Russia launched one of its biggest overnight attacks of the war on Friday, firing more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles,
articles.body: Ukraine said Russia launched one of its biggest overnight attacks of the war on Friday, firing more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, at several cities and regions.Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the barrage as one of the biggest attacks of the war, accusing Moscow of deliberately spacing out missile strikes to hamper rescue and recovery efforts. He said Russia fired missiles in successive waves, with gaps of 20 to 30 minutes, making it harder for emergency crews to extinguish fires, clear rubble and restore damaged infrastructure."There were people killed practically by the time specialists were inspecting the first damage to facilities and the Russians were launching follow-up strikes," Zelenskyy said in a post on social media.The strikes hit several cities and regions, damaging energy facilities, transport infrastructure and residential buildings. Zelenskyy said the targets included bridges across the Dnipro river, railway facilities, substations and power lines linked to Ukraine's nuclear power plants and electricity connections with neighbouring European Union countries.He said Russia also used missiles carrying cluster warheads, adding to the difficulty of responding to the attack. Emergency and repair work was underway across the country wherever security conditions allowed, with restoration deadlines set for affected regions.Ukraine says it intercepts 79 cruise missilesUkraine's air defence forces shot down 79 cruise missiles during the overnight assault, Zelenskyy said, praising the performance of Ukrainian combat aircraft, including F-16s, Mirages and MiGs.However, he said intercepting ballistic missiles remained significantly more difficult and depended on supplies from Ukraine's international partners.Ukraine's forces also targeted three Russian ballistic missile launchers during the night. One was destroyed, while the impact of strikes on the other two was still being assessed, Zelenskyy said.Zelenskyy called on Ukraine's partners to respond with concrete support rather than statements of solidarity, urging them to accelerate air defence deliveries.He said he had instructed Ukraine's foreign ministry to contact countries preparing new air defence packages and separately discussed supplies of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles with the defence minister. Kyiv is also counting on the US Pentagon to release the deliveries it has been expecting.Zelenskyy accused Russian president Vladimir Putin of ordering the attack to compensate for what he described as Moscow's diplomatic and military setbacks. He linked the strikes to Putin's recent meetings in China and said Russia was resorting to attacks on civilians amid weakening positions on the battlefield."Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic incapacity with precisely this kind of terror," he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘All our relationships will improve’: Pakistan minister in Delhi for SCO summit
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's federal minister for climate change and environmental coordination Musadik Masood Malik on Friday expressed hope that relations
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's federal minister for climate change and environmental coordination Musadik Masood Malik on Friday expressed hope that relations across the subcontinent, including between India and Pakistan, would improve, describing the inaugural Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum as a "tremendous opportunity" for multilateral engagement on shared history, culture and civilisation.Malik, who is leading the Pakistani delegation at the three-day forum being held at Purana Qila in New Delhi from November 20 to 22, said he hoped countries in the region would adopt a broader perspective and work towards advancing a common regional agenda."I think all of our relationships will improve. The region is in flux, as you know. The plates underneath geopolitics are shifting very fast. I'm very hopeful that we will take a macro view, and in that macro view, we'll be looking at all of the political issues, all of the social issues, all of the issues of conversation, and we'll be pushing the agenda of the region," Malik said when asked whether India-Pakistan relations could improve following the forum.Asked about India's concerns over cross-border terrorism, the Pakistani minister said, "I think tomorrow, once I give my statement, we'll have a lot of conversations..."On the civilisational links between India and Pakistan, Malik emphasised the importance of dialogue among countries with shared historical and cultural connections."I think dialogues are between distinct entities. Singularity doesn't require a dialogue. Singularity only requires a monologue. Dialogue is about diversity. I think between India, Pakistan, Russia, China and Central Asian states, if you go to the excavations, you would find that dialogue taking place just in the fore. I think it's a very welcome dialogue," he said.Describing the significance of the inaugural SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, Malik said the gathering offered an opportunity for countries to discuss their interconnected cultural and civilisational heritage."It is a tremendous opportunity for us to have a multilateral dialogue about civilisation. I think cultures and civilisations cut across boundaries, and it is fantastic that we are here and talking about our history, our geography, and our cultures and civilisations. It is a very welcome sign," he added.Malik arrived in New Delhi earlier on Friday and was received at the airport by Pakistan High Commission's Chargé d'Affaires Saad Warraich. His visit marks the first visit by a Pakistani minister to India in three years.According to Pakistan's ministry of foreign affairs, Malik is representing the country at the forum and is scheduled to participate in thematic sessions, where he will present Pakistan's perspective on the importance of inter-civilisational dialogue and its role in diplomacy.The inaugural forum has brought together participants from SCO member states, observers and dialogue partners to explore the region's shared civilisational heritage and strengthen cultural cooperation. India is hosting the three-day event to promote cultural exchange, mutual understanding and people-to-people ties among countries in the SCO region.Defence minister Rajnath Singh had announced India's plan to host the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum while addressing the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on October 20.The SCO has 10 member states, including India, Pakistan, China and Russia. India became a full member of the grouping in 2017.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
