articles.title: A 700-year-old English castle where Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn are said to have dined is up for sale for £5 million; it features a moat, medieval jousting yard and bear-baiting ring
articles.summary: Allington Castle, a more than 700-year-old English castle where King Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn are said to have dined, has been listed for sale for £5
articles.body: Allington Castle, a more than 700-year-old English castle where King Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn are said to have dined, has been listed for sale for £5 million. Located near Maidstone in Kent, the historic property features a moat, a medieval jousting yard, a bear-baiting ring and underground Dog Caves. Spanning approximately 42 acres along the River Medway, the estate also includes a Great Hall associated with the royal couple, historic gardens, and multiple accommodation buildings. Formerly owned by Sir Robert Worcester, the castle also operates as a venue for weddings, corporate events and film productions.Allington Castle features a medieval moat, jousting yard and Dog CavesAccording to Mansion Global, Allington Castle dates from between 1279 and 1299, with parts of the building dating back to the 12th century, and the property is mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086. The castle stands on approximately 42 acres of woodland, gardens and riverside grounds along the River Medway. Its historic features include a moat surrounding the building, a tilt yard used for jousting tournaments, a bear-baiting ring and underground spaces known as the Dog Caves.The bear-baiting ring was historically used for events in which bears and dogs were made to fight for spectators. The Dog Caves beneath the castle are believed to have housed hunting hounds or working dogs. The property also has two inner courtyards and retains features associated with its medieval past. The estate was once owned by the Wyatt family, who transformed the castle into a grand residence in the late 15th Century.Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn are said to have dined in Allington Castle's Great HallThe castle's Great Hall is associated with King Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, who are said to have dined there during their visits. The hall retains its historic character, with the property featuring thick stone walls, leaded windows and stately fireplaces. Knight Frank also states that Henry VIII stayed in the castle's Royal Room during his visits.Oli Streeter, an associate in Knight Frank's South East National Country Department, described the property as an opportunity to take responsibility for a significant historic estate. Speaking about the sale, he said it offered an “opportunity to become the custodian of a remarkable piece of English history”. According to the BBC, Streeter said that the family was “looking for the next custodian... to take on Allington for the next 20, 30, 40 years, just like Sir Robert”.Allington Castle's 26 reception rooms and nine lodgings add to its appealAlongside its medieval features, Allington Castle has living spaces that include a kitchen, dining room, sitting room, library and multiple bedrooms. Nine separate lodgings across the estate provide additional accommodation for family members, guests or staff. The castle has 30 bedrooms and 26 reception rooms.The property also operates as a venue for weddings, corporate events and film productions. The Great Hall can accommodate approximately 120 guests, while a converted barn can seat up to 150 people. The castle has also been used for television productions, including the children's historical comedy series Horrible Histories, which has filmed at the property several times. The Avengers was among the productions filmed there.Castle's grounds feature Italian gardens, kestrel nests and an historic dovecoteThe castle's approximately 42-acre grounds include formal gardens, ornamental fountains, woodland and a meadow. Kestrels nest in the castle towers and a historic dovecote, a structure built to house pigeons or doves, is believed to be among the oldest in England. The estate also has a large Victorian-style greenhouse and fruit and nut trees, including Kent cobnuts, apples, pears and plums.Other amenities include a tennis court, garages and an indoor swimming pool, which is currently not in use. The grounds include Italian Gardens and riverside moorings. The castle is not open to the general public, although it has hosted private events and weddings. Prospective buyers viewing the property can expect a tour lasting up to two hours because of the extensive grounds, Streeter told the BBC.Sir Robert Worcester restored Allington Castle after buying it in 1996Allington Castle was reportedly the longtime home of Sir Robert Worcester, who purchased the property in 1996. The castle had fallen into decline when Worcester acquired it, and he undertook restoration work to bring it back into use. The BBC reported that he lived there from the late 1990s until he died in 2025.Streeter told the BBC that Worcester had devoted considerable time to maintaining and restoring the property, including returning books and furniture that had been lost from the castle for centuries. His restoration work helped preserve the building's historic features and its character as a private residence. Following his death, the property was placed on the market for £5 million, with the family seeking someone to continue looking after the estate.Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available from the BBC and Mansion Global. The Times of India has not independently verified the property's historical details, features, ownership records, restoration work or current sale price. References to Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn dining at the castle are based on historical accounts and should not be interpreted as independently confirmed facts.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: US nonprofit chief Abraham Jaipaul Papabathini accused of sexually abusing minor girls in India; FBI seeks potential victims
articles.summary: The president of a Kansas City-based nonprofit organization that claims to help vulnerable children in India has been indicted on federal charges of
articles.body: The president of a Kansas City-based nonprofit organization that claims to help vulnerable children in India has been indicted on federal charges of sexually abusing minor girls during multiple visits to the country. Abraham Jaipaul Papabathini, 53, faces four federal counts of engaging in illicit sexual conduct with minors in India. A federal grand jury in Missouri returned the indictment, according to the US Department of Justice.Court documents alleged that Papabathini travelled to India several times between 2022 and 2024 and engaged in criminal sexual acts with girls aged between 14 and 17. Some of the alleged incidents took place in Chillakallu, Andhra Pradesh.Papabathini is the president of Rescuing Lives, a tax-exempt nonprofit organization that solicits donations to support children and widows in India. The organization describes its mission as rescuing vulnerable children and widows from streets and slums and providing them with secure facilities.According to court records, the organization operates a school in Visakhapatnam and an orphanage in Chillakallu. Its website says the facilities provide care for children aged between five and 16.A federal judge has ordered Papabathini to remain in custody while the case proceeds.FBI seeks potential victims, witnessesThe Federal Bureau of Investigation has launched an appeal for information from anyone who may have been victimized by Papabathini or has knowledge of his alleged conduct. The FBI's Child Exploitation Operational Unit is seeking to identify potential victims and witnesses, including people who may have information about attempts to engage in inappropriate sexual conduct. The Justice Department also issued a press release in Telugu, the native language where the NGO works.The agency has clarified that it wants information regardless of the age of the individuals involved or when and where the alleged incidents took place, including in the US, India or other countries.Potential victims, their guardians and anyone with relevant information have been asked to complete a confidential online questionnaire on the FBI's website. Investigators may contact respondents for further information.The FBI said Papabathini was arrested on November 7, 2026. A criminal complaint was filed on November 6, followed by a four-count indictment returned by a federal grand jury on November 17.The case is being investigated by the FBI's Child Exploitation Operational Unit, with assistance from its Kansas City Field Office. Papabathini faces up to 40 years in prison on each count if convicted.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: New York City proposes ban on restaurants boiling live lobsters, crabs and other crustaceans, with repeat violations attracting fines of up to $100 amid concerns over whether the creatures feel pain
articles.summary: New York City lawmakers have introduced a bill seeking to prohibit restaurants and other food-service establishments from putting live lobsters, crabs and
articles.body: New York City lawmakers have introduced a bill seeking to prohibit restaurants and other food-service establishments from putting live lobsters, crabs and other crustaceans directly into boiling water to cook them, bringing the treatment of marine animals under renewed scrutiny. The proposed legislation, introduced on November 19, 2026, argues that crustaceans may experience pain and distress when subjected to the practice without being stunned first. If passed, restaurants would still be allowed to serve lobster, crab and other crustacean dishes, but would have to use alternative preparation methods. Establishments violating the proposed restriction would receive a warning for their first offence, while repeat violations could attract civil penalties of up to $100.Why New York City wants to ban boiling lobsters aliveAnimal welfare concerns form the central argument behind the proposed legislation. Its sponsors have cited scientific research suggesting that lobsters, crabs and other decapod crustaceans possess the capacity to experience pain and distress.The supporting memorandum argues that putting these animals directly into boiling water without first stunning them can cause significant suffering. It also points to restrictions introduced in other countries and argues that restaurants should adopt preparation practices that minimise unnecessary harm.The debate has gained attention as scientific research increasingly examines the nervous systems, behaviour and responses of invertebrates that have traditionally received less consideration under animal-welfare laws.What does the proposed legislation say?The bill, identified as Introduction 1188-2026, was sponsored by New York City Council members Oswald J. Feliz and Harvey D. Epstein. It seeks to amend the city's Administrative Code by introducing a provision prohibiting food-service establishments from placing live crustaceans into boiling liquid for cooking or preparing them for human consumption.The proposed restriction covers aquatic invertebrates belonging to the crustacean group, including lobsters and crabs. Its wording is not limited to these two species, meaning other crustaceans intended for human consumption could also fall within its scope.The legislation would apply to restaurants and other food-service establishments, as well as owners, operators, employees and individuals acting on their behalf. It does not prohibit the sale or consumption of crustaceans or prevent restaurants from offering seafood dishes prepared using other methods.Restaurants could face fines for repeat violationsThe proposed legislation outlines a two-stage penalty system for establishments found violating the restriction.A restaurant committing a first violation would receive a notice explaining the alleged breach, along with a warning that subsequent violations could result in financial penalties. No monetary fine would be imposed for the first offence.However, a second or subsequent violation could attract a civil penalty of up to $100 for each offence. If the bill is approved and becomes law, the restrictions would come into effect 180 days after its enactment.What a major scientific review found about crustacean painA 2021 review commissioned by the UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) and conducted by researchers at the London School of Economics (LSE) examined more than 300 scientific studies on the sentience of cephalopods and decapod crustaceans.Led by researchers including Dr Jonathan Birch, the review assessed eight criteria associated with the capacity to experience feelings, including pain receptors, connections within the nervous system, protective behaviour, associative learning and responses to pain-relieving substances.The researchers found strong scientific evidence that decapod crustaceans, including lobsters, crabs and crayfish, are sentient and capable of experiencing pain, distress or harm.The report also recommended banning live boiling, among other slaughter methods, where more humane alternatives are available, unless the animals are first effectively stunned using electricity.Other countries have introduced animal-welfare protectionsNew York City's proposal follows a wider international discussion about the treatment of crustaceans in the seafood industry.Switzerland has introduced regulations requiring crustaceans to be stunned before they are killed, while Norway has also adopted restrictions concerning the boiling of live lobsters without prior stunning.The UK took a different legislative approach in 2022 when its Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act formally recognised decapod crustaceans, including lobsters and crabs, and cephalopod molluscs, including octopuses, as sentient animals. This recognition requires their welfare to be considered in relevant government decision-making, rather than imposing a blanket ban on boiling them alive in restaurants.Restaurant industry raises concerns over the proposalThe proposed restriction has also drawn criticism from some restaurant owners and hospitality industry figures in New York.Some restaurateurs have questioned the need for another regulation affecting food preparation, pointing to the financial pressures already facing the city's hospitality industry, including high rents, food costs, labour expenses and taxes.Some restaurant operators have also expressed concern that additional restrictions could complicate their operations and affect plans to open or expand businesses in the city.Supporters of the proposal, meanwhile, maintain that it would not remove lobster or crab from restaurant menus. Instead, establishments would have to change how they prepare the animals before cooking them.Introduction 1188-2026 was formally introduced in the New York City Council on November 19 and referred to its Committee on Health for consideration.The proposal must undergo the city's legislative process before it can become law. Until then, restaurants can continue using existing preparation methods, including boiling live crustaceans.If enacted, the measure would introduce a new animal-welfare requirement for food-service establishments while allowing customers to continue ordering lobster, crab and other crustacean dishes prepared using alternative methods.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel's new 'Super Ice' missile packs 4x the punch; why it's a perfect fit for India
articles.summary: Israel's Rafael Advanced Defense Systems has added a heavier hitter to its cruise missile family.
articles.body: Israel's Rafael Advanced Defense Systems has added a heavier hitter to its cruise missile family. Unveiled on November 11, Super Ice is a long-range missile designed for stand-off strikes against strategic targets. Its biggest upgrade is its warhead: at 1,000 lb, it is four times heavier than the 250 lb warhead carried by Ice Breaker, the missile it is based on.Super Ice will join Ice Breaker and Sea Breaker in Rafael's portfolio of long-range precision-guided weapons.Designed for launch from air, land and maritime platforms, the missile retains compatibility with Ice Breaker's launch systems, mission-planning infrastructure and logistics, allowing customers to add strike capability without replacing existing support equipment.According to The Jerusalem Post, Super Ice is compatible with Israel's main combat aircraft, including the F-35, F-16 and F-15. It features autonomous navigation, low-altitude terrain-following flight and all-weather capability. Its electro-optical guidance system uses image matching to maintain accuracy against a wide range of targets.Rafael has not disclosed the missile's range. However, Ice Breaker has a range of more than 300 km, suggesting Super Ice could reach farther.Where India comes inThe announcement has particular relevance for India. Ice Breaker is a low-level, terrain-following missile designed to skim at low altitude and resist electronic countermeasures. It can operate in GNSS-denied environments and uses an imaging infrared seeker, scene matching and automatic target recognition.The missile is about four metres long, weighs less than 400 kg and carries a 113 kg warhead. At Aero India 2025, Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) signed a memorandum of understanding with Rafael to manufacture Ice Breaker in India and customise it for the armed forces' requirements.Ice Breaker's external shape is similar to that of the Spice 1000, allowing aircraft already cleared to carry the Spice 1000 to accommodate the missile with relatively minor changes to avionics and store certification. The Indian Air Force's Mirage-2000, Su-30MKI and Tejas aircraft are currently equipped to carry the weapon.The Defence Acquisition Council cleared proposals worth around Rs 79,000 crore on December 29, 2025. The Air Force's share included Spice 1000 long-range guidance kits from Rafael and Astra Mk-II missiles. The kits are expected to expand the IAF's precision-munition stock for deep-strike missions.Reports citing an Israeli journalist have also claimed that India has ordered Air LORA, an air-launched ballistic missile developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), with a reported range of 400-430 km. Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) has signed an MoU with IAI to manufacture the missile in India. However, these orders have not been officially confirmed.What Super Ice could addThere is no indication yet that Super Ice is part of India's plans, and Rafael has not disclosed its range or detailed performance specifications. If India considers the missile in the future, its common architecture with Ice Breaker could offer an advantage, with BDL's existing work potentially providing a foundation for production and support.A heavier warhead could expand the range of targets the IAF could strike, including hardened facilities. For now, Super Ice reflects the direction of the stand-off weapons market: greater warhead power, compatibility with more launch platforms and the ability to add new capabilities without investing in entirely new infrastructure.

articles.title: Anant Ambani's Vantara airlifts seven-week-old elephant calf Raja from Assam for treatment
articles.summary: A seven-week-old elephant calf who has fought for survival since birth is being flown more than 2,500 km across the country for emergency treatment.
articles.body: A seven-week-old elephant calf who has fought for survival since birth is being flown more than 2,500 km across the country for emergency treatment. Raja, an Asian elephant calf, is being airlifted from Pohumara in Assam to Vantara in Jamnagar, Gujarat, where he will receive intensive hospital care. For the past seven weeks, a veterinary team from Vantara has been treating him at his owner’s home. However, his condition has now deteriorated to a point where hospitalisation offers the only real chance of recovery. With the calf too young and fragile to survive a road journey of over 2,500 km, an airlift was the only viable option.This isthe third airlift of its kind in India made possible by Anant Ambani, Founder of Vantara, who has stepped in to ensure that Raja reachesspecialised care quickly and safely."Raja came into this world with a broken leg, but not a broken spirit. For seven weeks, he has fought with a courage far bigger than his tiny body. Now it is our turn to carry him. With Anant Ambani's compassion and support, a journey that would take days by road will take just hours by air, and at Vantara we will give him every chance to stand, to walk, and one day to run." Vivaan Karani, CEO, Vantara.A difficult beginningRaja was born on 2 October 2026 at Gogamukh, Assam. His mother, only 11 years old herself, was young and inexperienced. Frightened and anxious after the birth, she kicked her newborn, and Raja suffered a complete fracture of his right femur, the large thigh bone of his hind leg, on his very first day.At an age when a calf should be taking his first wobbly steps beside his mother, Raja could not stand or bear weight on his legs. He also could not receive his mother's colostrum or milk, the first nourishment that gives a newborn elephant immunity and strength.Seven weeks of care at homeRecognising that the calf needed specialised care, Raja’s owner and caregivers reached out to Vantara for help. The organisation’s Rapid Response Team arrived on October 8, 2026.X-rays revealed a complete overriding fracture, a serious injury in which the broken ends of the bone slide past each other and fall out of alignment. The team stabilised Raja’s leg with a plaster cast and supportive bandaging, and used a sling to help him stand while keeping weight off the injured limb. He was also put on a specially formulated milk replacement, with feeding bottles provided and his caregivers trained on how to feed him.On October 10, Raja was shifted to his owner’s residence in Pohumara, where the Vantara team has since continued his treatment, nursing and round-the-clock monitoring. A hydrotherapy pond was also built near his resting area, allowing him to move and build strength without putting weight on the fracture.Why hospitalisation can no longer waitWithout his mother's milk and unable to move freely, Raja has faced one complication after another. He developed diarrhoea, and laboratory tests found a Klebsiella pneumoniae bacterial infection. He has had recurrent episodes of low blood sugar. Blood tests showed raised liver markers, pointing to stress on his liver. Long hours lying down have caused pressure sores on his head, and he also has an umbilical hernia and generalised weakness.The team has treated each of these with targeted antibiotics, intravenous fluids, liver support, vitamins and minerals, probiotics, wound care and careful nutrition. But Raja's condition remains serious. He now needs what can only be provided in a fully equipped hospital: advanced diagnostics, continuous monitoring, specialist orthopaedic care, and a structured nutrition and rehabilitation programme.The journeyRaja is departing today on a specially arranged flight from Guwahati to Jamnagar, a journey of about four hours. He is travelling in a crate designed especially for him, sized to his small body and built to keep his fractured leg stable and supported, lined with deep, soft bedding to cushion him and protect his pressure sores through take off, flight and landing. A dedicated team of Vantara veterinarians, paravets and caregivers is staying by his side for the entire journey, continuously monitoring his heart rate, breathing, temperature, hydration and blood glucose, with fluids, medication and milk feeds ready on board. Moving him by air means hours instead of days in transit, reducing stress and risk for a calf whose body has very little reserve.What awaits Raja at VantaraOn arrival, Raja will be admitted to Vantara's elephant hospital, where veterinarians will carry out a full diagnostic assessment and continue pain management, medication, mobility therapy and nutritional rehabilitation. Given the nature of his injury, he is expected to need lifelong veterinary care and monitoring, and Vantara is committed to providing it. It is heartening to see Anant Ambani support the rescue of a critically ill baby elephant, enabling the calf to be airlifted to Vantara for specialised treatment and a chance at recovery.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: We all know that feeling when a sudden long weekend opens up for us, with no professional or social obligations to fulfil.
articles.body: We all know that feeling when a sudden long weekend opens up for us, with no professional or social obligations to fulfil. The expanse of extra time stretching ahead feels delicious and we want to make the most of it!Next time such a magical window opens up, consider Dubai. Just under four hours away from India, you’d be surprised to know just how calming and relaxing a Dubai getaway can be.Wellness and urban eleganceSunlight streams in through the expansive windows at One&Only One Za’abeel, an architectural marvel that feels suspended in the clouds.Within this serene enclave, the Longevity Hub by Clinique La Prairie offers advanced, science-led treatments to coax the body into a state of wholesome wellbeing.If one goes from Za’abeel street to Marasi Drive, The Lana, Dorchester Collection stands welcoming guests with understated elegance. One can drift through the sunlit corridors into the exclusive Dior Spa The Lana, surrendering to highly personalised therapies that melt away the stresses of the outside world: the perfect mood reset before an unhurried stroll through nearby designer boutiques.Another fascinating experience is Contrast Therapy - which, in the past few years, has moved from niche athletic recovery to a mainstream wellness and biohacking staple across the city. Alternating between warming and cooling environments, these sessions allow the body to recharge naturally. Give it a go and reset your mind and body for an enchanting evening of Michelin-starred dining under the city lights.Whispering waves and beachfront serenityTrading the cityscape for the endless Arabian Gulf reveals a completely different rhythm. The ocean provides a natural, lulling soundtrack to a day of absolute leisure. Imagine emerging from a bespoke, rejuvenating treatment at Atlantis The Royal's AWAKEN facility, only to spend the afternoon floating in the quiet seclusion of a private luxury cabana, enveloped by the coastal breeze and the gentle afternoon sun.Further along the pristine coastline, Six Senses The Palm, Dubai blooms as a holistic sanctuary devoted entirely to longevity and gentle movement. The property intertwines bespoke spa therapies with serene fitness routines, creating a space where the outside world fades away. Nearby, Jumeirah Al Qasr brings cutting-edge innovation into its tranquil setting, focusing on deeply restorative rituals like red-light therapy at the renowned Talise Spa.For those seeking absolute privacy, the Bvlgari Spa at Bvlgari Resort Dubai and the Guerlain Spa at One&Only The Palm elevate traditional hammam rituals into immersive, personalised journeys.Complementing these shoreside havens, Mandarin Oriental Jumeira, Dubai and Four Seasons Resort Dubai at Jumeirah Beach offer expansive, sun-drenched relaxation spaces. The residential side of these properties flow seamlessly into elegant luxury shopping arcades, allowing you to drift between wellness and exclusive retail at your own pace and convenience.Mindful immersion and tranquil desert isolationTrue wellness often blossoms when we step entirely off the familiar path. Dubai nurtures profound mental resets through deeply immersive, unconventional therapies designed to awaken the senses. articles.title: Planning a wedding near IGI Airport? Delhi Police bans laser beams at farmhouses, banquet halls, hotels in Palam area till Jan 16, citing risk to pilots and passengers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has banned the use of laser beams during weddings, parties and other celebrations in areas under the Palam subdivision of the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has banned the use of laser beams during weddings, parties and other celebrations in areas under the Palam subdivision of the Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport, citing the risk of pilots being distracted while landing aircraft.The order, issued by assistant commissioner of police Pradeep Kumar Meena under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, came into force on November 18 and will remain effective until January 16, 2027.According to the order, the Air Traffic Control (ATC) at IGI Airport had reported several incidents in which pilots experienced visual distractions due to laser beams, particularly during aircraft landings.Such incidents not only cause nuisance but can also pose a serious threat to the safety of passengers, crew members and aircraft, it said.Police said several farmhouses, banquet halls, hotels and restaurants had come up in and around the airport area, where bright lights, including laser beams, were frequently used during weddings, parties and other events."The use of such beams, particularly in open spaces during night hours, has emerged as a concern as they can directly affect the vision of pilots operating aircraft. In order to prevent danger to human life and ensure the safety of aircrafts, it is necessary to take immediate measures to regulate the use of laser beams in and around IGI Airport," the order said.The ban covers individuals, groups, event organisers, owners, occupiers and employees of banquet halls, hotels, restaurants, buildings and other properties within the Palam subdivision's jurisdiction."Anyone found violating the order will be liable for action under Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with disobedience to orders duly promulgated by public servants," read the order.(With inputs from PTI)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Halloween is a time to remember dead brands
articles.summary: I became addicted to Britannia’s Petit-Beurre biscuits back in the early 1990s.
articles.body: I became addicted to Britannia’s Petit-Beurre biscuits back in the early 1990s. I had started working in Mumbai and was living in paying-guest accommodation. These converted servant quarters rarely had kitchen access, so you had to make do with an electric kettle and ready-to-eat foods.Biscuits were ideal, but which? Marie and Parle-G were sweet and boring, Monaco too salty and cream crackers made a crumbly mess. Petit-Beurre were perfect. They had a delicious buttery taste, neither too salty nor sweet and were firm enough to eat without problems. A packet was breakfast. Then Britannia discontinued them. For weeks I stalked kirana stores for their last packets.Since then, I have discovered that Petit-Beurre still exists, in different places. As the name indicates, it was originally French, first created in 1886 by the Lefèvre-Utile company in Nantes, in a region known for good butter. Other companies copied it, down to its rectangular shape with tiny ‘ears’ at each corner which, by tradition, French children always bite off first.The original company, now part of Mondelez, still makes it abroad. Some Indian companies also make it, including Britannia, which now calls it Marie Gold Petit Beurre, the kind of corporate confusion you get when the brand manager is probably already looking for another job. I’ve tried some of these Indian versions, and none are quite what I remember eating.In the run-up to Halloween, all dead and not quite dead things are in vogue. We should include dead brands and the zombie versions can linger on. Dead brands can elicit an emotional response that more than qualifies them for the festival. I learned this many years back when I did a story for ET on why companies discontinue brands and how small groups of consumers continue to long for them.As part of the story, I asked friends and colleagues which brands they missed. I was flooded with responses: Double Cola, Appela, Do It and Thrill soft drinks; Cookie Feast and Cream Puff biscuits; Lipton Covo chocolate spread, Polson’s butter, Kwality’s Black Magic frozen desserts. Then the story was printed and so many readers wrote in with memories of dead brands that we printed two more stories just from these responses.The dead brands weren’t all edible. Several people recalled toothpastes, like Signal, Kolynos and Forhans, though perhaps taste played a role here too. Smokers recalled cheap cigarettes like Blue Bird and Guinea Gold which they probably started smoking with. A Goan friend recalled her aunts insisting she hunt through Mumbai for Libertina bras. Many readers recalled this brand as well, a testament to the brand power that personal comfort brings.But food brands easily led the list, a sign perhaps of how readily food companies rationalise their portfolios, despite consumer feelings. There have been several examples of food brands being revived due to consumer outcries, which are easily amplified on the Internet. In the US, for example, Hostess Twinkies, small, cream filled cakes were known, rather dubiously, for almost never going bad. Health concerns lead to declining sales and the company producing them went bankrupt in 2012. But outcry at their impending extinction led to the brand being bought and other companies producing them, with just a few months gap. Reliance’s relaunch of Campa is an attempt to build on this appeal.Companies are sometimes willing to do special production runs for devoted customers, but this can backfire. The eccentric billionaire Howard Hughes was known for eating Baskin-Robbins banana-nut ice-cream every day. When his staff learned that the flavour was being discontinued, they paid Baskin-Robbins to do a special production run. A few weeks later, Hughes suddenly switched to French vanilla, and his staff was left with gallons of banana-nut ice-cream. They were, apparently, eating it for years. A banana-nut themed Halloween costume might seem unusual, but it would be a testament to the curious power of dead brands.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
articles.summary: This prolonged execution comes weeks after Christa Pike survived the lethal injection of the same drug.
articles.body:
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.

This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.

His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.

When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".

He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."

Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.

"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"

The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murder, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.

Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".

The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.

articles.title: Myanmar genocide verdict divides world, opens Pandora's box for Israel
articles.summary: A genocide verdict against Myanmar may have delivered a historic moment for the Rohingya, but its biggest shockwaves could be felt far beyond the
articles.body: A genocide verdict against Myanmar may have delivered a historic moment for the Rohingya, but its biggest shockwaves could be felt far beyond the country's borders.The International Court of Justice's (ICJ) decision holding Myanmar responsible for genocide has opened a legal Pandora's box, putting Israel's ongoing genocide case over Gaza under renewed scrutiny and exposing a growing divide among the world's major powers over the authority of international courts.While Europe has rallied behind the verdict, United States has struck a cautious note, raising questions over the court's interpretation of international law.The ICJ on Thursday found Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during the military crackdown in Rakhine state in 2017. The verdict, delivered in a case brought by The Gambia in 2019, marks the first time the UN's highest court has held a state responsible for genocide, making it a landmark moment in international law.The ruling has triggered sharply contrasting reactions, with the United States adopting a cautious position while the European Union has thrown its weight behind the court.A US state department spokesperson said Washington was examining the judgment, stressing that the proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention was of paramount importance and that the ICJ should not be politicised.Washington also reiterated its support for Myanmar's people and expressed "grave concerns" over continuing human rights abuses against Rohingya Muslims and other minority groups. The state department highlighted the US role as the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya crisis response.The European Union, in contrast, described the verdict as a landmark judgment and called on Myanmar to implement it without delay. An EU spokesperson said compliance with ICJ decisions was "not optional" but an obligation under international law, reaffirming the bloc's support for the court's role in upholding the international legal order.Myanmar, however, rejected the ruling, with its military-backed government questioning the verdict's legitimacy. Presidential spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe described the decision as "unfair", pointing to the 9-6 split among the 15 judges."When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision. So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair," she told reporters at a press conference in Naypyidaw on Friday.Myanmar's military rulers have consistently denied committing genocide, maintaining that the 2016-17 operations in Rakhine state were counter-terrorism operations targeting the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), which had carried out insurgent attacks. The ICJ, however, rejected Myanmar's argument that the military campaign was primarily a counter-terrorism operation.Russia's position came into focus after Myanmar invoked a joint declaration issued by US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping following their November 19 meeting.The declaration stated that the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies "must not abuse their jurisdiction", emphasising respect for state sovereignty and immunity for state officials.Myanmar's presidential spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe cited the declaration while questioning the authority of international judicial institutions following the ICJ verdict. However, Moscow has not issued a separate statement on the Myanmar judgment.China, meanwhile, directly raised concerns over the ICJ's approach. Foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing was concerned about "jurisdictional overreach and expanded interpretation", arguing that such practices were not conducive to resolving disputes.He called on the international community to work together to avoid complicating the issue, while reiterating China's support for dialogue and efforts to facilitate the repatriation of displaced Rohingya from Rakhine state.Israel in the crosshairsThe legal Pandora's box opened by the Myanmar verdict could have its biggest implications for Israel. The ICJ is already hearing a genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its military offensive in Gaza, and the historic finding against Myanmar could now add another layer to the legal battle.Israel has strongly rejected the allegations, maintaining that its military campaign is aimed at Hamas and not the Palestinian population.The significance lies in how the court examined Myanmar's defence. The military rulers in Naypyidaw had argued that their operations in Rakhine state were aimed at countering insurgents. The ICJ, however, assessed the wider pattern of military conduct and the evidence of killings, sexual violence and destruction of Rohingya villages to determine whether genocidal intent could be established.This reasoning could become relevant when the court examines Israel's arguments that its operations in Gaza are driven by security objectives.The ruling has also put Washington in a politically uncomfortable position. The US has backed Israel throughout the Gaza war and has repeatedly criticised international legal proceedings against its ally.Its cautious response to the Myanmar verdict, particularly its warning against politicisation of the ICJ, raises a larger question about how it would react if the same court eventually reaches an adverse finding against Israel.However, the Myanmar judgment does not automatically decide Israel's case. South Africa's proceedings remain pending, and the court will have to independently assess the evidence against Israel.The bigger question is whether the legal principles applied to Myanmar will carry the same weight when the country facing allegations is a close ally of the world's most powerful nation.You use AI every day.
